title: Intraguild interference and biocontrol effects of generalist predators in a winter wheat field
experiment_type: field exclusion (predator removal within open enclosures)
location: FAM experimental farm, Scheyern, Southern Bavaria, Germany (~40 km north of Munich)
design: 2×2 factorial: carabid removal (yes/no) × spider removal (yes/no) within stainless-steel enclosure rings (0.5 m², dug 5 cm into soil, 20 cm above ground, open top — no mesh cover except during sampling). Four treatments each replicated 7 times: (1) carabids reduced — carabid beetles removed by pitfall trapping and hand search, spiders present; (2) spiders reduced — lycosid and linyphiid spiders removed, carabids present; (3) both reduced — carabids and spiders both removed; (4) none reduced — unmanipulated control. Predator removal by live-catching pitfall traps (first week) then manual search every 2nd day (~15 min per enclosure). Two replicates excluded per removal treatment due to insufficient removal success, leaving n = 5 per removal treatment and n = 7 for control. Enclosures in a 5 × 7 grid (3 m apart) in a 17 × 25 m plot, 100 m from field margin. Season: 24 May to 4 August 1995.
notes: Removal treatments n = 5 (2 replicates excluded each); control n = 7 (no exclusions). The 'none reduced' (unmanipulated) treatment is the natural/ambient predator control. Grain mass reported as 'mg per ear' in Table 3, but values (~2.1) are almost certainly in grams per ear — 2.1 mg per ear is biologically implausible for wheat; a wheat ear typically yields ~1–2 g of grain. Reported as printed, flagged as likely unit error. The SE for 'Both reduced' grain mass (0.38) appears unusually large compared to other treatments (0.02–0.05); possible typographical error. Carabid removal led to a significant increase in grain protein content (F₁,₁₈ = 6.25, P < 0.05, Table 3: carabids reduced 9.25 ± 0.10%, both reduced 9.60 ± 0.17%, vs spiders reduced 9.03 ± 0.11%, none reduced 9.16 ± 0.11%) — not extracted as a separate outcome since grain protein is a quality metric, not yield or damage. Cicadellidae and Delphacidae (leafhoppers + planthoppers) showed no significant treatment effects (P > 0.30, Fig. 6C,D) — not extracted due to non-significance and very small bar differences on a 0–4 scale. Spider removal DECREASED Thysanoptera densities (counter-intuitive) — paper attributes this to indirect effects through intraguild predation cascades (removing spiders releases other predators from spider predation, increasing predation on thrips). Statistical analyses used 2 × 2 factorial repeated-measures ANOVA (General Linear Model with Pillai's Trace); data were log(x+1)-transformed. Values presented are means ± SE throughout.

figure_read.evidence_note: Fig 4B p6; third bar (Both reduced, cross-hatched); bar top slightly below the 5 tick → ~4.0. Error bar cap extends to ~7. Control (None reduced): ~5.0. Direction: full predator removal DECREASES aphids — counter to expected top-down cascade. Checked: bar identities confirmed from legend (Both reduced = ▼ symbol, third position). This counter-intuitive result is the paper's central finding — intraguild interference means removing all predators does not simply release pests. A trend toward an interaction between carabid and spider removal was detected (F₁,₁₈ = 3.53, P = 0.07). Precision ± 1 unit.

observations.notes: Counter-expected direction: full predator removal produces fewer aphids than ambient control. Checked: bar identity confirmed, values read correctly. The paper's Discussion explains this through intraguild interference — removing carabids releases lycosid spiders from predation/competition, which then exert stronger predation on aphids. The interaction term F₁,₁₈ = 3.53, P = 0.07 (two-tailed) suggests a trend toward non-additive predator effects. n_control = 7.
